abstract: Abstract High-risk carcinogenic human papillomaviruses (HPVs), e.g. HPV16, express the E6 and E7 oncogenes from two mRNAs that are generated in a mutually exclusive manner by splicing. The HPV16 E7 mRNA, also known as the E6*I/E7 mRNA, is produced by splicing between splice sites SD226 and SA409, while E6 mRNAs retain the intron between these splice sites. We show that splicing between HPV16 splice sites SD226 and SA409 is controlled by a splicing enhancer consisting of a perfect repeat of an adenosine-rich, 11 nucleotide sequence: AAAAGCAAAGA. Two nucleotide substitutions in both 11 nucleotide sequences specifically inhibited production of the spliced E6*I/E7 mRNA. As a result, production of E7 protein was reduced and the ability of HPV16 to immortalize human primary keratinocytes was abolished. The splicing-enhancing effect was mediated by the cellular TRAP150/THRAP3 protein that also enhanced splicing of other high-risk HPV E6*I/E7 mRNAs, but had no effect on low-risk HPV mRNAs. In summary, we have identified a novel splicing enhancer in the E6 coding region that is specific for high-risk HPVs and that is critically linked to HPV16 carcinogenic properties.

To construct subgenomic HPV16 plasmids pX550, pX525, pX502 and pX438, HPV16 sequences were first amplified by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) from pC97ELsL with primers B97S and X556A, X550A, X525A, X502A and X438A, respectively. To generate plasmids pX478AW+M, pX478AM+W and pX478AM+M, HPV16 sequences were first PCR-amplified from pC97ELsL with primers B97S and X478AWT+mut, X478Amut+WT and X478Amut+mut, respectively. To generate plasmids pX478AM1, pX478AM2, pX478AM3, pX478AM4 and pX478AM5, HPV16 sequences were first PCR-amplified from pC97ELsL with primers B97S and X478AM1, X478AM2, X478AM3, X478AM4 and X478AM5, respectively. The PCR fragments were digested using Fast Digest enzymes Ptel and Xhol (Thermo Scientific) and cloned into the pCL086 vector digested with the same restriction enzymes. To generate plasmids pX478sM1, pX478sM4 and pX478midM, Phusion site-directed mutagenesis (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used with 5′-phosphorylated primers, P-pX478M-Rv and P-sM1-Fw, PsM4-Fw and P-middleM-Fw, respectively. To generate plasmids pX478 SA409OPT and pX478 SA409OPT+M1M4 from plasmid templates pX478 and pX478M1M4, respectively, Phusion site-directed mutagenesis was used with 5′-phosphorylated primers P-SA409OPT-Rv and P-SA409OPT-Fw. Sequences of PCR primers used for plasmid constructions are listed in
Supplementary Table S1
.
To generate plasmids with mutations at the identified enhancer in pC97ELsL, a two-step PCR mutagenesis was performed. In the first two PCRs, one outer primer (pC97Sall or B97+HPV16 Sbfl) and one inner primer (478M1M4AS PCRmut or 478M1M4S PCRmut) were used in each reaction, with inner primers containing the mutations. Primers are listed in
Supplementary Table S1
. This first PCR resulted in two PCR fragments with overlapping fragments, which could base-pair. These two PCR fragments were diluted 1:100 and a second PCR using the two outer primers was performed. This resulted in a longer PCR fragment containing mutations in the center of the fragment. The PCR fragments were digested with Fast Digest enzymes Sall and Sbfl (Thermo Scientific), and cloned into the pC97ELsL plasmid digested with the same enzymes, resulting in pC97M1M4. To generate pC97ELsL M2, the DNA fragment encoding the HPV16 genomic sequence nucleotides 104–881 was purchased from Eurofins Genomics Llc. The mutant HPV16 sequence was amplified by PCR using primers pC97SalI and B97+HPV16 SbfI followed by subcloning into SalI and SbfI sites of pC97ELsL.
The mutations of the enhancer in pHPV16AN were constructed by ordering plasmids containing sequences between the two unique restriction sites Bglll and Sbfl in the pHPV16AN plasmid. The Bglll–Sbfl fragment encompassed the splicing enhancer and contained the four nucleotide substitutions representing the M1 and M4 mutations. The mutant fragments were ordered from Eurofins Genomics LIc. These plasmids were digested with BgllI and Sbfl (Thermo Scientific) to release the mutant DNA sequence that was subsequently inserted into pHPV16AN plasmid digested with the same enzymes, resulting in pHPV16ANM1M4.

The primer sequences are listed in
Supplementary Table S1

The chimeric HPV16 E6- and E7-encoding plasmids in which the splicing enhancer between HPV16 nucleotide positions 444 and 475 in plasmid pC16HAE6E7F was replaced with the corresponding sequence from HPV6b, HPV31, HPV18 or HPV45, were generated by the Phusion site-directed mutagenesis kit (Thermo Scientific) using the following pairs of 5′-phosphorylated primers: P-Enh1.16to6b-F and P-Enh1.16to6b-R, P-Enh1.16to31-F and P-Enh1.16to31-R, P-Enh1.16to18-F and P-Enh1.16to18-R, or P-Enh1.16to45-F and P-Enh1.16to45-R. The sequences of the primers are listed in
Supplementary Table S1
. These mutagenesis reactions resulted in plasmids pC.Enh1.16to6b, pC.Enh1.16to31, pC.Enh1.16to18 and pC.Enh1.16to45. To generate pC.Enh1.16to6b-17A#2, -19A#2 and -21A from pC.Enh1.16to6b, Phusion site-directed mutagenesis was performed using 5′-phosphorylated primers, P-Enh1.16to6bR and P-Enh.1.6b-17#2-Fw, -19A#2-Fw or -21A-Fw, respectively. To generate pC.Enh1.16to6b-17A#3, -19A#3 and -21A#2, Phusion site-directed mutagenesis was performed using P-Enh1.16to6b-R2 and P-Enh.1.6b-17#2-Fw, -19A#2-Fw or -21A-Fw, respectively.
All plasmids used in this study have been sequenced to confirm their identity and are available upon request.
Cells
HeLa, 293T, SiHa and C33A cells were cultured in Dulbecco's modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM; Cytiva, previously Hyclone) supplemented with 10% bovine calf serum (BCS; Hyclone) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Gibco). The normal neonatal human foreskin primary keratinocytes [nHFKs (HEKn, PCS-200–010)] were purchased from ATCC and grown in EpiLife medium (Gibco) with 1% human keratinocyte growth supplements (HKGS, Gibco) and 0.2% gentamicin/amphotericin (Gibco). This medium was also used for propagation of the immortalized human keratinocyte cell line JJM9721 established here by stable transfection of HFKs with pC97ELsL. The HeLa, SiHa and JJM9721 cell lines used here have been subjected to the Cell Line Authentication Test (Eurofins Genomics).
Transfections
Transfection of HeLa cells was performed using Turbofect according to the manufacturer's instructions (Thermo Scientific). Transfections of 293T, SiHa and C33A cells were carried out using Fugene6 (Promega). nHFKs (PCS-200–010, ATCC) were transfected using Xfect (TaKaRa Bio). Cell culture medium was changed 6 h post-transfection. All plasmids were transfected in a minimum of three independent experiments.
siRNA and siRNA transfections
SiHa and JJM9721 cells were transfected using ON-TARGET SMARTpool small interfering RNA (siRNA) from Dharmacon using Dharmafect1 (Dharmacon), according to the manufacturer's protocol. The scrambled control (si-scr) was siGENOME Control pool non-targeting #2 (D-001206–14–20, Dharmacon™). siRNA to TRAP150 was ON-TARGETplus Human THRAP3 (GeneID: 9967) siRNA-SMARTpool (L-019907–00–0020) and siRNA against BCLAF1 was ON-TARGETplus Human BCLAF1 (GeneID: 9774) siRNA SMARTpool (L-020734–00–0005).
RNA extraction and RT–PCR
Total RNA of HeLa was extracted using TriReagent (Sigma) and the Direct-zol RNA Miniprep kit (Zymogen Research), according to the manufacturer's instructions. Total RNA of other cell lines was extracted using TriReagent (Sigma) and chloroform (Sigma), according to the manufacturer's instructions. DNase I (Sigma) treatment was performed in solution at 37°C for 1 h, followed by phenol–chloroform–isoamyl alcohol (IAA) extraction and ethanol precipitation. A 1 μg aliquot of total RNA was reverse transcribed at 37°C for 50 min in a 20 μl reaction using the M-MLV reverse transcriptase (Invitrogen) and random hexamer primers (Thermo Scientific). A 1 μl aliquot of the newly synthesized cDNA was used in a PCR amplification assay. Reverse transcription–PCR (RT–PCR) products were pre-stained with GelRed and subjected to DNA agarose electrophoresis. RT–PCR primers are listed in
Supplementary Table S2
.
RNA fractionation
Nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions were obtained using the NE-PERTM Nuclear and Cytoplasmic Extraction Reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer's protocol. Nuclear and cytoplasmic RNA were extracted by TriReagent and chloroform as described for RNA extraction, followed by DNase I treatment and cDNA synthesis.
Real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR)
A 1 μl aliquot of cDNA was used in the qPCR analysis using StepOnePlus (Applied Biosystems) with the SsoAdvanced SYBR Green Supermix (Bio-Rad) in line with the manufacturer's instructions. To quantify human telomerase reverse transcriptase (hTERT) mRNA levels, primers hTERT-F and hTERT-R were used. TRAP150 mRNA levels were determined using primers TRAP150QFw and TRAP150QRv. BCLAF1 mRNA levels were determined using primers BCLAF1qFw and BCLAF1qRv. Intron retained (IR) E6 and spliced 226^409(E6*I) mRNA levels were determined using primers E6QF and 234AS or E6*I-F and E6*I-R, respectively. The locations of primers are indicated in Figure
1B
. The results were normalized to glyceraldehyde phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) mRNA levels determined using primers gapdhs and gapdha. qPCR primers are listed in
Supplementary Table S2
.
RNA oligo-mediated protein pull-down assay
HeLa nuclear extracts were prepared according to a previously described method (
39
). To extract cytoplasmic proteins, cells were lysed using buffer I [10 mM HEPES pH 7.9, 10 mM KCl, 0.1 mM EGTA, 1 mM dithiothreitol (DTT), 0.2% NP-40 and protease inhibitor] followed by centrifugation. The supernatants were stored as cytoplasmic extracts, while the nuclear pellets were resuspended in buffer II (10 mM HEPES pH 7.9, 400 mM NaCl, 1 mM EGTA, 1 mM EDTA, 1 mM DTT and protease inhibitor) to extract nuclear proteins. For RNA oligo pull-down assay with TRAP150-depleted lysates, cells were transfected with siRNAs targeting TRAP150 or BCLAF1 or with scrambled control RNA followed by preparation of nuclear extracts at 72 h post-transfection. In some cases, the nuclear extracts were further purified on HiTrap Q-columns. Flow-through fractions were collected, while proteins in the column were subjected to step-wise elution with 50 mM, 200 mM or 1 M KCl. A 60 μg aliquot of nuclear extract was mixed with 1 mg (100 μl) of magnetic streptavidin-coated beads (Dynabeads M-280 Streptavidin, Invitrogen) pre-incubated with 200 pmol of single-stranded biotin-labeled RNA oligonucleotides in Binding buffer (10 mM HEPES pH 7.9, 2.5 mM MgCl
2
, 0.5% Triton X-100, 150 mM NaCl and 1 mM DTT). The sequences of the RNA oligos are listed in
Supplementary Table S3
. Incubation with RNA oligo-covered beads was performed at room temperature for 40 min followed by washing 10 times with 500 μl of ice-cold binding buffer (10 mM HEPES pH 7.9, 2.5 mM MgCl
2
, 0.5% Triton X-100, 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM DTT). Proteins were eluted using 2× Laemlli buffer and subjected to sodium dodecylsulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS–PAGE) followed by either western blotting or silver staining.
Preparation of proteins for mass spectrometry
Proteins pulled down using RNA-mediated protein pull-down assay were separated by SDS–PAGE and stained using silver stain (SilverQuest™ staining Kit, Invitrogen). Bands appearing stronger in pull-downs with wild-type HPV16 RNA oligos compared with protein bands observed after pull-down with mutant HPV16 RNA oligos were excised from the gels. The bands were subjected to proteolytic cleavage and liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis at the SCIBLU Proteomics Resource Center at Lund University.
Preparation of proteins and western blotting
Total cellular protein was extracted by resuspension of cells in radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) buffer (50 mM Tris pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 1.0% NP-40, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate, 0.1% SDS, 2× protease inhibitor and 1 mM DTT) followed by over-end rotation at 4°C for 30 min and centrifugation to remove cell debris. To perform western blotting, protein extracts were subjected to SDS–PAGE and western blotting as described previously (
39
). The filters were stained with primary antibodies and subsequently with horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibodies followed by signal development with the Super Signal West Femto chemiluminescence substrate (Thermo Scientific) and detection in ChemiDoc MP (Bio-Rad) or with IR-conjugated secondary antibodies followed by detection in Odyssey CLx Imager (LI-COR). Antibodies are listed in
Supplementary Table S4
.
RNA–protein immunoprecipitation (RIP) assay
Cells were resuspended in 1 ml of non-denaturing cell lysis buffer (20 mM Tris–HCl pH 8, 137 mM NaCl, 1% IGEPAL CA 630, 2 mM EDTA, 2× protease inhibitor, RNase inhibitor) and passed through a 19-gauge needle to sheer the DNA. The samples were incubated with over-end rotation at 4°C for 30 min followed by centrifugation to remove the cell debris. Five percent of each lysate was stored for later to be used as input samples. In the immunoprecipitation, 50 μl of protein G Dynabeads (Thermo Scientific) and 1 μg of antibody were incubated with 500 μl of pre-cleared cell lysate with over-end rotation at 4°C for 2 h. Antibodies used are listed in
Supplementary Table S4
. Following incubation, the beads were washed eight times using wash buffer (20 mM Tris–HCl pH 8, 137 mM NaCl, 1% IGEPAL CA 630, 2 mM EDTA) and RNA was extracted using using Trizol-chloroform, followed by DNase I treatment (Sigma), purified by phenol–chloroform–IAA and precipitated by ethanol. The precipitated RNA was resuspended in 22 μl of ddH
2
O and 10 μl was reverse transcribed using M-MLV reverse transcriptase (Invitrogen) and random hexamer primers (Thermo Scientific) according to the manufacturer's protocol. A 1 μl aliquot of cDNA was subjected to PCR amplification using the primers indicated in each figure.
Co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP)
Transfected 293T cells were lysed using 1 ml of non-denaturing lysis buffer (20 mM Tris–HCl pH 8, 137 mM NaCl, 1% NP-40, 2 mM EDTA, 2× protease inhibitor) for 20 min with over-end rotation at 4°C followed by centrifugation to remove the cell debris. When RNase treatment was indicated, RNase A (final 5 μg/ml, Thermo Scientific) was added followed by incubation for 15 min at room temperature prior to centrifugation. In parallel, Protein G Dynabeads were washed twice followed by incubation with 1 μg of antibody and three washing steps. The cell lysate was pre-cleared by incubation with Protein G Dynabeads without antibody for 30 min at 4°C with over-end rotation; 5% of the cell extract was stored as input sample. The remaining cell lysate was divided into control, to which IgG was added, and pull-down sample, to which either anti-FLAG or anti-U2AF65 antibody was added and incubated overnight, after which they were washed six times prior to SDS–PAGE and western blotting.
Induction of immortalization of primary human keratinocytes
Immortalization of nHFKs was assayed by transfection of HPV16 subgenomic plasmids followed by selection of cells resistant to calcium- and serum-dependent differentiation, as described previously (
40
). Briefly, subconfluent nHFKs growing on 100 mm plates were either untransfected or transfected with pC97ELsL or pC97M1M4 using Xfect transfection reagent according to the manufacturer's protocol (as briefly described above). At 24 h after transfection, cells were transferred to 150 mm plates and grown in EpiLife medium. After cells reached confluency, the cells were selected in DMEM supplemented with BCS (10%) and penicillin–streptomycin (1%) to induce differentiation. The cells were grown in the selection medium for 8 weeks, at which time point selection was terminated. The selected cells were resistant to induction of keratinocyte differentiation and showed continuous proliferation. At that stage, only cells transfected with pC97ELsL were proliferative and were transferred back into serum-free EpiLife medium (= passage 15 at that stage). The cells were grown and passaged alongside non-transfected nHFKs (= passage 4 at that stage) to obtain a population doubling curve to demonstrate immortalization of the transfected cells. The population doubling level (PDL) was calculated using the formula: PDL = 3.32[log (total viable cells at harvest/total viable cells at seed)]. In parallel, cells were harvested at extra passages 0, 2, 4 and 9 for the evaluation of hTERT expression as determined by RT-qPCR. The pC97ELsL-immortalized cell line was named JJM9721.
Subconfluent nHFKs (passage 5) growing on 100 mm plates were transfected with pUC (neomycin selection control), pRSVneo, pHPV16AN, pHPV16ANM1M4, pHPV16AN+ pCAGGS-nlscre (Cre recombinase) or pHPV16ANM1M4+pCAGGS-nlscre (Cre recombinase), respectively. At 24 h post-transfection, the cells were split 1:4 into a new plate to avoid high cell confluency, followed by neomycin selection with 40 μg/ml G418 for 3 days and in 10 μg/ml for an additional 3 days. After selection and expansion, the cells were frozen as liquid nitrogen stocks with the same cell number (passage 8 at that time). After thawing, cells were seeded on 6-well plates followed by recovery on 100 mm plates for cultivation and subjected to selection using DMEM with 10% BCS as described above. After 11 weeks of selection, colony formation caused by HPV16 plasmid transfection was documented by cell fixation and staining with crystal violet solution [0.05% w/v Crystal Violet (Sigma), 1% formaldehyde, 1% methanol, phosphate-buffered saline (PBS)] for 20 min at room temperature. Transfected cells frozen in liquid nitrogen were revived and passaged 0, 2 and 4 times, followed by RNA extraction and evaluation of hTERT expression determined by RT-qPCR.
Water-soluble tetrasodium (WST)-1 cell viability assay
SiHa cells were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 4 ×10
3
, 8 × 10
3
or 16 × 10
3
cells/well. Cells were transfected the following day, either with control vector (pUC19) or with increasing concentrations of pTRAP150. Cell viability was measured at 24 or 48 h post-transfection. Cell culture medium was replaced with fresh growth medium at 2 h prior to the WST-1 assay. WST-1 assay reagent (Roche) was added to a final concentration of 10% of the cell culture medium followed by incubation for 0.5–4 h at 37°C in 5% CO
2
. The absorbance of the formazan product was measured at 450 nm using a TriStar Plate Reader (Berthold Tech).
UV-cross-linking and RNA oligo-mediated protein pull-down assay
The method for RNA oligo-mediated protein pull-down assay was modified as the RNA oligo and nuclear extract proteins were UV-cross-linked prior to washing and elution steps. A 60 μg aliquot of HeLa nuclear extract was incubated with 200 pmol of biotinylated single-stranded RNA oligonucleotide in Buffer D (final concentration: 15 mM HEPES pH 7.6, 80 mM KCl, 2.4 mM MgCl
2
, 0.15 mM EDTA, 8.5% glycerol and 0.2 mM DTT) for 10 min at room temperature. The mixtures were UV-cross-linked with 800 mJ/cm
2
at 254 nm. The UV-cross-linked mixtures were then incubated with 1 mg of Dynabeads M280-Streptavidin in Binding buffer-2 (10 mM HEPES pH 7.9, 2.5 mM MgCl
2
, 4 mM KCl, 0.5 mM EGTA, 0.5 mM EDTA, 0.5% Triton X-100, 3% glycerol, 150 mM NaCl and 1 mM DTT) for 30 min at room temperature. Following incubation, the beads were washed eight times using Binding buffer with different concentration of sodium chloride (10 mM HEPES pH 7.9, 2.5 mM MgCl
2
, 0.5% Triton X-100, 150/300/600/1000 mM NaCl as indicated in the figures and 1 mM DTT). After washings, the proteins were eluted using 2× Laemmli buffer and subjected to SDS–PAGE and western blotting. For RNA oligonucleotide sequences, see
Supplementary Table S3
.
Sequence alignment
Jalview version 2.11.2.5 was used for multiple sequence alignments.
Quantitation
Image Lab 6.0.1 software was used to determine band intensity on chemiluminescent western blot and RT-PCR images. ImageJ 2.3.0 software was used to determine band intensity on immunofluorescent western blot images.
Statistics and reproducibility
Each experiment was carried out at least in triplicate with reproducible results. Quantitative analysis and Student
t
-tests (unpaired, two-tailed test) were performed using Prism GraphPad Prism 9.

Introduction
The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) has deemed 15 human papillomaviruses (HPVs) carcinogenic to humans (
1
,
2
). HPV16 is the most common carcinogenic, high-risk HPV (HR-HPV) (
https://pave.niaid.nih.gov/
). In contrast, low-risk HPVs (LR-HPVs) are not associated with cancer. During the HPV life cycle, E6 and E7 proteins are required for generation of an intracellular environment that is permissive for HPV DNA replication (
3–6
). The E7 protein promotes cell proliferation, primarily by interacting with members of the pocket protein family including Retinoblastoma protein (pRB) in a manner that liberates transcription factor E2F (
7
). The E6 protein on the other hand binds to p53 via E6-AP and causes ubiquitin-mediated degradation of p53, thereby preventing apoptosis of the HPV-infected cell (
8
). HR-HPV E6 and E7 are notorious in the sense that they are responsible for induction and maintenance of cancer caused by HR-HPVs and are defined as viral oncogenes (
9–13
). HR- and LR-HPVs differ in the mode of E6 and E7 gene expression. While LR-HPVs utilize two independent promoters to produce E6 and E7 mRNAs, the HR-HPVs produce E6 and E7 from two alternatively spliced mRNAs generated in a mutually exclusive fashion from the same pre-mRNA (Figure
1A
,
B
) (
14
). The E6 mRNA is generated by retention of an intron that encodes E6, while the E7 mRNA is generated by splicing that removes the upstream E6-encoding intron (Figure
1A
,
B
) (
https://pave.niaid.nih.gov/
). This spliced mRNA named E6*I/E7 mRNA is diagnostic for HR-HPV types and is the major and most abundant E7-producing mRNA (Figure
1A
,
B
) (
15
). Indeed, the levels of the E6*I/E7 mRNA gradually increase during progression of HPV16 infections to cervical cancer (
16–18
). Furthermore, E6 and E7 mRNAs are affected by chemotherapeutic drugs (
19
), suggesting that they may be targeted for therapy to HPV infections, including malignancies caused by HPV .
Figure 1.
Identification of a splicing enhancer in the HPV16 E6-coding region that is required for production of 226^409-spliced E7 mRNA. (
A
) Schematic representation of the HPV16 genome. The early genes E6, E7, E1, E2, E4 and E5 are depicted as white boxes and the late genes L2 and L1 as gray boxes. The early and late promoters P97 and P670, respectively, are indicated as arrows. pAE and pAL indicate early and late polyadenylation signals, respectively. The splice donors are indicated with black ovals and the splice acceptors as white ovals. The number beneath each splice donor and acceptor indicates their nucleotide position in the HPV16 reference genome (GenBank ID:
K02718.1
). LCR, long control region. (
B
) Representative alternatively spliced mRNA variants produced from the HPV16 genome are shown. The IR E6 and 226^409-spliced HPV16 mRNAs are highlighted in red. Arrows indicate HPV16-specific reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) and real time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) primers in this study. The right panel describes the RNA isoform structures of the HPV16 IR E6 mRNA (upper image) and the 226^409-spliced E6*I/E7 mRNA (lower image). The IR E6 mRNA consists of the E6 cistron from HPV16 nucleotide number 104–559, a two nucleotide non-coding spacer region (nucleotides 560–561) and the E7 cistron (nucleotides 562–858) both with their own start and termination codons, followed by the 5′ end of downstream E1 cistrons. The 226^409-spliced mRNA consists of the E6*I cistron including nucleotides 104–226 spliced to nucleotides 409–417, a 144 nucleotide non-coding spacer region (nucleotides 418–561) and the E7 cistron (nucleotides 562–858). 226^409 splicing results in an out-of -frame fusion of the E6 coding region of the first exon to the second exon. (
C
) Schematic representation of the HPV16 subgenomic plasmid pX1200 and an overview of HPV16 sequences present in the various deletion mutant plasmids. The E6, E7 and part of the E1 gene are depicted as white boxes. The splice donors are indicated with black ovals and the splice acceptors as white ovals. All plasmids start at nucleotide position 97 of the HPV16 genome but end at various positions indicated in the plasmid names to the left. Black arrow, human cytomegalovirus (CMV) immediate early promoter. Positions of the RT-PCR primers 97S and 438A are indicated. (
D
) RT-PCR on RNA extracted from HeLa cells transfected with plasmids displayed in (C). RT-PCR primers 97S and 438A were used to detect both IR E6 (top band) mRNAs and mRNAs spliced between SD226 and SA409 (226^409, lower band). gapdh was used as a control. M, marker. (
E
) The percentage of 226^409-spliced HPV16 mRNAs is plotted against the endpoint of each HPV16 deletion mutant displayed in (C). The band intensities of IR E6 and 226^409 mRNAs obtained from (D) were quantified by Image Lab 6.1 Software (BioRad). The percentage of spliced 226^409 mRNA was calculated by dividing the values of 226^409 by the sum of IR E6 + 226^409 values multiplied by 100. Mean values and standard deviations are shown. The putative splicing enhancer between HPV16 nucleotides 438 and 478 is indicated. All data are representative of three biologically independent experiments.
The HPV16 splice sites used for production of the spliced E6*I/E7 mRNA are named SD226 and SA409 in HPV16 (Figure
1A
,
B
) (
20–24
). Since E6 and E7 are both essential proteins in the HPV life cycle and are both required for initiation and maintenance of cancer, it is of paramount importance to maintain an optimal ratio between intron retention and splicing between SD226 and SA409 to produce sufficient quantities of both E6 and E7. Therefore, splicing between SD226 and SA409 must be strictly controlled to avoid over- or undersplicing. SA409 has an interrupted polypyrimidine tract (underlined):
CCGUUGUGUGAUUUGUUAAUU
AG/GUGUA. This indicates that SA409 is a suboptimal splice acceptor that may require an additional mechanism to produce E6*I/E7 mRNAs. RNA-binding proteins that inhibit splicing between SD226 and SA409 and cause intron retention have been identified, i.e. hnRNP A1 (
25
,
26
), hnRNP D (
27
) and hnRNP G (
28
). In sharp contrast, the cellular
trans
-acting factor(s) and HPV RNA elements that are required for splicing between SD226 and SA409 to produce the major E6*I/E7 oncogene mRNA remain unidentified.
In this work, we sought to define the molecular mechanism for production of the HPV16 oncogenic E6*I/E7 mRNA. We identified a splicing enhancer element named ENH-1 that spans 32 nucleotides, and is located 35 nucleotides downstream of SA409. It consists of an adenosine-rich 11 nucleotide perfect repeat with a 10 nucleotide spacer. Introducing just twonucleotide substitutions in ENH-1 resulted in the abrogation of the splicing between SD226 and SA409. Additionally, we identified TRAP150/THRAP3 (thyroid hormone receptor-associated protein complex 150 kDa component/thyroid hormone receptor-associated protein 3) as a
trans
-acting factor that interacts with the ENH-1 sequence and mediates the splicing between SD226 and SA409. TRAP150 has previously been shown to regulate cellular mRNA alternative splicing and spliced mRNA nuclear export (
29–33
), but evidence has been lacking regarding which
cis
-RNA element TRAP150 interacts with to regulate mRNA alternative splicing. Here we show that TRAP150 interacts with HPV16 ENH-1 in
in vitro
RNA oligo pull-down assay and in living cells, and recruits U2 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (snRNP) auxiliary factor 65 kDa, U2AF65 to ENH-1. The effect of TRAP150 on the induction of E6*I/E7 mRNA splicing was also observed in other HR-HPVs, but not in LR-HPVs. Our results allow us to propose a model in which HPV16 ENH-1 and TRAP150 are critical for regulating the expression of the viral E6 and E7 oncoproteins at the level of RNA processing and contribute to the carcinogenic properties of carcinogenic HPVs.

Identification of a
cis
-regulatory RNA element (ENH-1) that is required for HPV16 226^409 splicing and production of the high-risk HPV-specific E6*I/E7 mRNA
The mRNAs encoding the E6 and E7 oncogenes of HR-HPVs are produced in a mutually exclusive manner. An IR E6 mRNA encodes the complete E6 coding sequence (CDS), whereas the spliced E6*I/E7 mRNA encodes a truncated E6 (E6*I) as well as the complete E7 CDS (Figure
1A
,
B
). In HPV16, the E6*I/E7 mRNA is produced by splicing between the 5′-splice site SD226 and the 3′-splice site SA409, both situated within the E6 CDS (226^409 splicing, hereafter) (Figure
1A
,
B
;
Supplementary Figure S1A–C
). To identify
cis
-RNA elements that are required for HPV16 226^409 mRNA splicing, a series of HPV16 deletion mutants with HPV16 sequences of varying length downstream of SA409 were constructed (Figure
1C
) and transfected into the cervical cancer cell line HeLa. The activation of 226^409 splicing was monitored using RT-PCR with primers that amplify both IR E6 and 226^409 cDNA of different amplicon sizes (Figure
1C
). In the smallest plasmid that ends at HPV16 nucleotide position 438, 226^409 splicing was not observed (Figure
1D
), indicating that enhancer elements regulating splice acceptor SA409 were located downstream of nucleotide 438. When HPV16 sequences present in the plasmid were extended further with another 40 nucleotides to HPV16 nucleotide position 478, splicing to SA409 increased from 0% to 80% (Figure
1D
,
E
), indicating that a strong splicing enhancer element was present within the 40 nucleotides between HPV16 nucleotide positions 438 and 478. The splicing enhancer was tentatively named enhancer-1 (ENH-1). Additionally, our results suggested the existence of multiple
cis
-RNA regulatory elements that induce or reduce splicing to SA409. One of these RNA elements has been characterized as a splicing silencer element encoding a UAG-containing sequence located between HPV16 nucleotides 599 and 601 (
25
). However, in the present study, we focus on the potential splicing enhancer ENH-1 as it is currently unclear how splicing of the HPV16 226^409 (E6*I) mRNA is activated.
The
cis
-acting RNA splicing element downstream of the HPV16 splice site SA409 (ENH-1) contains an 11 nucleotide perfect repeat
The region between HPV16 nucleotide positions 438 and 478 contained a sequence of 11 nucleotides perfectly repeated twice (Figure
2A
,
B
: pX478). When mutating either the second, first or both of these 11 nucleotide repeats, splicing to SA409 was significantly reduced (Figure
2C
). Next, two nucleotides at a time were mutated in both repeats simultaneously (Figure
2B
, M1–M5). Splicing to SA409 was reduced in all mutant plasmids compared with wild-type control, indicating a role in splicing for all 11 nucleotides in both repeats (Figure
2D
), although the nucleotide positions mutated in pX478M2 appeared to be less important for splicing enhancement. When mutating two nucleotides of M1 in the first or of M4 in the second 11 nucleotides (sM1 or sM4, respectively), splicing to SA409 was significantly reduced (Figure
2E
). Mutating the 10 nucleotides between the first and second 11 nucleotide motifs (midM) also reduced splicing to SA409 (Figure
2E
). These results indicated the importance of the identified ENH-1 region for HPV16 226^409 mRNA splicing regulation.

8

41

42

Replacement of the HPV16 ENH-1 with corresponding sequences from other high-risk HPVs maintained 226^409 splicing, whereas replacement with corresponding sequences from low-risk HPVs did not
E6*I/E7 mRNA splicing is specific for carcinogenic HR-HPVs. To determine if ENH-1 is conserved among HR-HPVs, the HPV16 ENH-1-encoding region was aligned with other HPV types. The alignment revealed that none of HR-HPVs except HPV16 encoded a perfect 11 nucleotide repeat sequence (
Supplementary Figure S5A, B
). However, the adenine (A) richness of the sequences corresponding to the first and the second 11 nucleotide repeats of HPV16 was conserved in the HR types (
Supplementary Figure S5A, B
). The A content of the first 11 nucleotide sequence was on average 73% for the HR-HPVs, whereas the A content of the second 11 nucleotide sequence was on average 66% for the HR-HPVs (
Supplementary Figure S5C
). Intriguingly, sequences corresponding to the two 11 nucletide repeats in LR-HPVs were also A rich, but to a lower extent (65% and 44% for the two 11 nucleotide repeats, respectively). The A content of the corresponding sequences in LR-HPVs was significantly lower than the A content of the HR-HPVs, in particular for the second 11 nucleotide repeat (
Supplementary Figure S5C
). The spacer sequence between the two 11 nucleotide repeats had an A content of 28% and 32% in HR- and LR-HPVs, respectively (
Supplementary Figure S5C
). Our results suggested that the high A content of the 11 nucleotide repeat sequence was a defining property of the splicing enhancer of the HR-HPVs (
Supplementary Figure S5D
).
To determine if sequences corresponding to HPV16 ENH-1 in other HR-HPVs possessed 226^409 splicing enhancer activity, 32 nucleotides of HPV16 sequences encompassing HPV16 ENH-1 (nucleotides 444–475) were replaced by corresponding sequences from other HR-HPVs (HPV31, HPV18 and HPV 45) or LR-HPV (HPV6b) in the HPV16 E6E7-encoding plasmid pC16HAE6E7F (Figure
3A
,
B
). The influence of the HR-HPV or LR-HPV sequences on HPV16 226^409 splicing was monitored by RT-PCR. The results revealed that 226^409 splicing was maintained at a relatively high level between 14% and 37% when HPV16 ENH-1 was replaced by sequences from other HR-HPVs (Figure
3C
,
D
), while 226^409 splicing was reduced from 34% to 3% when the HPV16 ENH-1 was replaced by LR-HPV (HPV6b) sequences (Figure
3C
,
D
). Considering the sensitivity of 226^409 splicing to just four nucleotide substitutions in HPV16 ENH-1 (Figure
2D
,
I
), it was to some extent surprising that replacement of HPV16 ENH-1 with the relatively divergent sequences from other HR-HPVs also supported splicing to SA409. By contrast, LR-HPV sequences did not significantly enhance splicing. We concluded that sequences from different HR-HPVs that correspond to HPV16 ENH-1 possessed splicing enhancing activity, whereas the corresponding sequence from an LR-HPV did not.

TRAP150 alters HPV16 E6/E7 mRNA splicing in HPV16-positive cervical cancer cells, thereby reducing cell viability
Usage of the HPV16 3′-splice site SA409 results in an mRNA coding for the E6*I and E7 proteins. The 226^409-spliced E6*I/E7 mRNA is the major producer of E7 protein (
15

7A

TRAP150 enhances 226^409 mRNA production through the interaction with ENH-1 and the recruitment of U2AF, thereby up-regulating E7 protein levels, while simultaneously reducing IR E6 mRNA levels and E6 protein production. Although the increased E7 protein levels may enhance cell proliferation, this may be counteracted by reduced E6 protein production and restoration of p53 followed by apoptosis. Thus, a balanced splicing of HPV16 226^409 would be of paramount importance in the HPV16 replication cycle as well as during carcinogenesis.

Discussion
Although not universally true, the majority of known splicing enhancers are purine rich (
45
), sometimes adenosine rich (
46
). The existence of splicing enhancers is not easily predicted based on sequence analysis as a result of positional effects, RNA secondary structure, the relative promiscuity of RNA-binding proteins and combinatorial effects (
47
). Thus, experimental results are required to unequivocally identify splicing enhancers. The HPV16 splicing enhancer element (ENH-1) identified here represents a perfect 11 nucleotide repeat with an adenosine content of 73% (Figure
2A
). Alignment with various HR-HPV sequences revealed that none of them had perfect bipartite repeats, but all had bipartite high A content regions (
Supplementary Figure S5
). Compared with the corresponding sequences in LR-HPVs, the HR-HPV ENH-1 sequences had a significantly higher adenosine content. This was particularly striking in the second 11 nucleotide repeat in which HR-HPVs had an average A content of 66% whereas LR-HPVs had an average A content of 44%. In contrast, the adenosine content of the first 11 nucleotide motif was more similar between HR- and LR-HPVs (74% in HR-HPVs versus 65% in LR-HPVs). Finally, the spacer sequence between the two repeats had a similar adenosine content in LR- and HR-HPVs (average 30%), approaching the generally expected 25% (
Supplementary Figure S5
). Taken together, these results suggest that the splicing enhancer in the high-risk types may have arisen evolutionarily by the accumulation of adenosine in the region corresponding to the second 11 nucleotide repeat in HPV16 and the other HR-HPVs.
Although our data clearly indicate that the A richness of the two 11 nucleotide repeats is a defining property of the splicing enhancer in HR-HPV types, we believe that A richness itself it is not sufficient to generate a splicing enhancer. Some degree of higher sequence complexity is clearly needed. For example, positions 5 and 6 in the 11 nucleotide A-rich repeat appear to tolerate a variety of substitutions in the various HR-HPV types (
Supplementary Figure S5A, B
) and the ‘G’ nucleotide at position 10 is strictly conserved among the HR-HPV types. In addition, the 10 nucleotide spacer sequence in between the 11 nucleotide A-rich repeats shows that four nucleotide positions are strictly conserved among high-risk types whereas the remaining six nucleotides may vary. Thus, A richness in combination with strictly conserved A or non-A nucleotides are likely to define the splicing enhancer. Considering the multiple RNA processing factors that interact with ENH-1, we speculate that the entire ENH-1 region, including the 10 nucleotide spacer, act in concert as a ‘landing pad’ for multiple splicing factors including TRAP150, PSF and RBM15 that contribute to the control of HPV16 226^409 splicing.
In addition to ENH-1, the deletion analysis in Figure
1
revealed that sequences downstream of ENH-1 also appear to affect splicing between SD226 and SA409. However, mutating ENH-1 was sufficient to significantly reduce splicing between SD226 and SA409 in the E6 coding region regardless of the downstream elements. These results established that ENH-1 is essential for HPV16 226^409 splicing. One may speculate that the downstream sequences represent splicing-modulatory elements or act on RNA secondary structure in such a way that splicing between SD226 and SA409 is affected, but their true significance remains to be determined. The presence of multiples positive and negative factors that interact with the
cis
-RNA regulatory elements (ENH-1 and possibly others) and the presence of splicing acceptor sites proximal to SA409 (SA526 and SA742) support the idea that multiple control mechanisms are in place, and postulate that dynamic structural changes could occur in both proximal and distant RNA regions, perhaps influenced by protein–protein, protein–RNA and RNA–RNA interactions. As a result, the formation of spliceosomal complexes could shift between the splice acceptors and affect which splice acceptor choice is made within the HPV16 E6/E7 gene region. Our experimental system in this study was simplified to primarily focus on the regulation of 226^409 mRNA splicing, limiting our ability to fully comprehend the complexity of HPV16 mRNA splicing.
An enigmatic result that appeared from this study was that the four nucleotide substitutions in the splicing enhancer (M1M4) that virtually abolished production of spliced E6*I/E7 mRNAs without major effects on the IR E6 mRNAs not only reduced production of E7 protein as predicted, but also dramatically reduced the levels of E6 protein (Figure
2K
;
Supplementary Figure S1F
). RNA analysis after cell fractionation revealed that IR E6 mRNAs carrying the M1M4 mutations displayed an RNA export defect that resulted in low E6 protein levels (
Supplementary Figure S3C
). It has been reported that purine-rich splicing enhancers present on unspliced mRNAs interact with nuclear factors that retain these mRNAs in the nucleus, a process that is relieved by splicing (
48
). On the other hand, our results demonstrated that the association of TRAP150 with the M1M4 mutant HPV16 mRNAs was impaired (Figure
6B
,
C
). TRAP150 has been reported to facilitate the RNA export of spliced mRNAs by interacting with the mRNA, exon junction complex components and the export receptors (
30
,
33
). These results may indicate that mutational inactivation of splicing enhancer ENH-1 deprives the mRNA of TRAP150 or other ENH-1-associated factors necessary for further mRNA processing including RNA export. Alternatively, it may indicate that RNA stability of the M1M4 mutant mRNAs in the cytoplasm was attenuated by an unidentified mechanism. These results may imply that TRAP150 has different effects on IR mRNAs and spliced mRNAs, and modulates the RNA levels in the nucleus and cytoplasm differently. Although our results indicate that TRAP150 is an alternative splicing regulator, we could not entirely exclude that TRAP150 might affect RNA stability and/or the efficiency of RNA nuclear export of individual alternatively spliced mRNAs to achieve the same results. Lee
et al.
reported that TRAP150-associated unspliced pre-mRNAs are destined to get degraded in the nucleus (
30
). The observed decrease in E6 mRNA and protein levels by TRAP150 expression could potentially be explained by TRAP150-mediated degradation of IR E6 mRNAs in the nucleus. However, quantitation of IR E6 mRNA and spliced E7 mRNA in the absence or presence of TRAP150 demonstrated that an increase in spliced E7 mRNA levels compensated for the reduction in IR E6 mRNAs, indicating that the reduction in the levels of IR E6 mRNAs in the presence of TRAP150 was caused by an increase in splicing rather than increased degradation of E6 mRNAs mediated by TRAP150. Nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) of HPV mRNAs has not been extensively researched. Further experimentation is required to determine if NMD contributes to the control of E6/E7 gene expression. It is of interest to determine how HPV16 E6 protein levels were reduced when ENH-1 was mutated and how TRAP150 differently regulates IR E6 mRNAs and spliced E7 mRNAs post-splicing.
The presence in the ENH-1 element of multiple consecutive adenosines (A-tracts) led us to speculate that ENH-1 may be targeted by poly(A)-binding protein (PABP) or adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADAR). In fact, PABPN1 was identified in our MS analysis following ENH-1 RNA oligo pull-down assay (
Supplementary Figure S6C
). Western blotting demonstrated that nuclear PABP (PABPN1) was pulled down by the wild-type ENH-1 RNA oligo but not with the mutant RNA oligo (
Supplementary Figure S14
). Recent studies have revealed novel functions for PABPN1 that include regulation of RNA splicing, and RNA degradation and export (
49
,
50
). It is of interest to further investigate if PABPN1 is a splicing regulator specific for HR-HPV E6/E7 mRNA splicing. Besides PABPN1, the A-to-I editing ADAR1 enzyme acts on adenosines. ADAR1 appears to be a prognostic factor for cervical cancer (
51
). One study reported that HPV16 E7 protein levels in SiHa were enhanced by ADAR1 knockdown (
52
). However, this effect was apparently mediated by the innate immune system rather than A-to-I editing, as no A-to-I editing was detected on HPV transcripts.
HR-HPVs [two HR-HPVs from the alpha-7 species (HPV18 and HPV45) and two from the alpha-9 species (HPV16 and HPV31)] analyzed in this study responded to TRAP150 overexpression with increased splicing, despite displaying bigger sequence divergence in the corresponding enhancer elements than that between HPV16 wild-type and M1M4 mutant enhancer. One may speculate that TRAP150 targets adenosine-rich, bipartite-like RNA elements, possibly interrupted by 1–3 non-adenosine residues. TRAP150 was initially identified as a spliced mRNP-associated protein (
53
), but an RNA-binding motif in TRAP150 has not been identified to our knowledge. However, the N-terminal RS domain of TRAP150 has been shown to contribute to the regulation of alternative splicing by an unknown mechanism (
31
). Both TRAP150 and BCLAF1 contain SR-domains. Many of the serine–arginine-rich (SR) proteins interact with purine-rich RNA elements to enhance splicing (
45
). We showed that the effect of TRAP150 was enhanced by BCLAF1 (Figure
7D
). In this regard, it is of interest to note that BCLAF1 is mutationally inactivated in ∼40% of HPV-positive tonsillar and base of tongue cancer (
54
), suggesting that the absence of BCLAF1 may alter HPV16 E6/E7 mRNA splicing in these cancers.
The correlation between TRAP150 and cervical cancer development remains to be elucidated. In this report, we suggest a model in which TRAP150 promotes HPV16 E6*I/E7 alternative splicing and E7 protein production via interactions with the identified HPV16
cis
-acting RNA element ENH-1, thereby effectively controlling and upholding an optimal balance of HPV16 E6 and E7 oncogene expression. TRAP150 overexpression did enhance E7 mRNA and protein levels, but resulted in reduced cell viability, presumably due to reduced E6 production caused by ‘over splicing’ of the E6/E7 pre-mRNAs (Figure
7A
). In fact, it has been reported that both E6 and E7 protein expression is required for HPV-induced cell immortalization
in vitro
(
55
). RNA-seq results from 169 HPV-positive cervical cancer samples revealed that all cancer samples had detectable expression of both HPV E6 and E7 mRNAs (
56
). On the other hand, it has been shown that the spliced E6*I/E7 mRNA is overexpressed in high-grade lesions and cancer caused by HR-HPV infections, and therefore potentially could serve as a biomarker for women at risk of progressing to cancer (
16
,
17
,
57
,
58
). Furthermore, high expression of E6*I/E7 spliced mRNA was shown to predict poor response to treatment of cervical cancer (
59
). Based on the results presented here, we suggest that the E6*I/E7 mRNA splicing is increased due to dysregulated expression of TRAP150 and that it may be of interest to determine the utility of TRAP150 as a biomarker for cancer progression or treatment response. Indeed, TRAP150 is part of the DNA damage response induced by HPV (
43
,
60
). Both TRAP150 and BCLAF1 are highly expressed in the cervical epithelium, with higher staining in the basal and middle cell keratinocyte layers than in the upper differentiated cells (
www.proteinatlas.org
). In summary, interactions between TRAP150 and the HPV16 ENH-1 RNA element are critical for HR-HPV pathogenesis, demonstrating that both TRAP150 and the splicing enhancer ENH-1 may be exploited as targets for therapy to treat high-grade lesions or cancer caused by HR-HPV infections, or as diagnostic or predictive biomarkers.
